title: Does the next half take as long?
hook: Half gone in 10 minutes. Is the next half gone in 10 more?

knows: that a half-life is the time for half of something to go (half-life lesson)
doesNotKnow: that for some reactions the half-life is not fixed: it lengthens as the reactant thins

misconception: Every reaction has one fixed half-life.
objective: The learner can explain that a second-order reaction that halves from 80 to 40 mmol/L in 10 min takes 20 min to halve again (then 40 min), because two molecules must meet and meetings get rarer as the reactant thins, while a first-order reaction keeps one half-life.

claims.text: A second-order reaction that takes 10 min to go from 80 to 40 mmol/L takes about 20 min to go from 40 to 20 mmol/L, and about 40 min more to reach 10 mmol/L.
claims.source: Integrated rate law 1/[A] = 1/[A]0 + kt: k = (1/40 - 1/80)/10 = 1/800 L/(mmol min); t(20) - t(40) = (1/20 - 1/40) x 800 = 20 min; t(10) - t(20) = 40 min (node; Demo.tsx timeTo()).

claims.text: A second-order reaction's half-life grows as the concentration falls; each half takes twice as long as the last.
claims.source: t1/2 = 1/(k[A]0) for rate = k[A]^2 (Atkins & de Paula, Physical Chemistry, ch. on chemical kinetics, table of integrated rate laws). | REVISION v2 2026-10-14: text edited to match stage; needs re-check.

claims.text: A first-order reaction keeps one fixed half-life (here 10 min each time); radioactive decay is first order.
claims.source: t1/2 = ln 2 / k, independent of concentration (Atkins & de Paula, ch. on kinetics). Radioactive decay is first order (IUPAC Gold Book, 'half life'). | REOPENED 2026-10-14 (v3, wave D r5 revision by demo-builder): learner-visible sentence changed; needs a fresh check. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 22): Pass 22 re-check of v3: own Euler integration of dA/dt = -kA (k = ln2/10): waits 10.00, 10.00, 10.00 min; t1/2 = ln2/k has no concentration term. "Radioactive decay is first order" confirmed only via web-search snippets of general-chemistry texts (LibreTexts/Averill 14.5); Atkins and the IUPAC Gold Book entry were NOT opened (hosts blocked).

claims.text: In a second-order reaction of this kind, two reactant molecules must meet, so the rate goes with the concentration squared; halving the concentration makes meetings four times rarer (rate 1/4 of the start after one halving, 1/16 after two). In first order the rate halves each time.
claims.source: Rate = k[A]^2 for an elementary bimolecular step 2A -> products (Atkins & de Paula, ch. on kinetics). Order is measured, not always from the equation; the lesson's reaction is stated to be second order. | REVISION v2 2026-10-14: text edited to match stage; needs re-check. | REOPENED 2026-10-14 (v3, wave D r5 revision by demo-builder): learner-visible sentence changed; needs a fresh check. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 22): Pass 22: rate = k[A]^2: (1/2)^2 = 1/4, (1/4)^2 = 1/16; first order 1/2, 1/4. Matches rate() readout in Demo.tsx. Own integration of dA/dt = -kA^2 (k = 1/800): waits 10, 20, 40 min. | REOPENED 2026-10-14 (v4, wave E r6 revision by demo-builder): rate values now shown as per-order rate rows (2nd: 1/4 → 1/16; 1st: 1/2 → 1/4) that the reveal quotes; needs a fresh check against the rows. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 24): VERIFIED. Derivation: second order in A means rate = k[A]^2 (mass action for a bimolecular step: meetings scale with [A]·[A]); halving gives (1/2)^2 = 1/4, then 1/16; first order 1/2, 1/4. Own node: waits 10, 20, 40 min (2nd) and 10, 10, 10 (1st). Rate rows rateRow() print '1/4 → 1/16' and '1/2 → 1/4'; gate guarantees seen[2] >= 2 and seen[1] >= 2 before reveal. Atkins not opened; not needed for the definition.

claims.text: Each halving leaves half as much to lose; in 2nd order it goes at a quarter of the rate, so the wait doubles; in 1st order at half the rate, so the wait stays the same. (Stage line: 'Each halving: ½ as much left to lose, at ¼ the rate → 2× the wait' / '... at ½ the rate → same wait'.)
claims.source: Scaling: for rate = k[A]^m, the time to go from c to c/2 scales as c^(1−m) (integrated rate law). m = 2: halving c doubles the wait; m = 1: the wait is unchanged. The rate at the start of each halving is (1/2)^m of the one before, which is the 1/4 or 1/2 on the line. The amount lost per halving is c/2, half the previous. Stage text in Demo.tsx (.why line). | Added 2026-10-14 (v3) by demo-builder. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 22): Pass 22: derivation. Each halving of a power-law decay is the previous one rescaled: concentration x1/2 at every matching point, so rate x(1/2)^m throughout; time = amount/rate scales by (1/2)/(1/2)^m = 2^(m-1): x2 for m = 2, x1 for m = 1. Exact, not an approximation. Matches the .why line text in Demo.tsx and own integration (c4).

recall.question: A second-order reaction takes 5 min to fall from 100 to 50 mmol/L. About how long does the next fall, from 50 to 25 mmol/L, take?
recall.why: For a second-order reaction the half-life is 1/(k[A]); halving [A] doubles it.
